questions.question: Explain why the Sun is classified as a star. State its distance from the Earth in kilometres and in light minutes, and compare its size and temperature with other stars.
questions.expected_answer: The Sun is a huge ball of hot gas, mainly hydrogen and helium, that produces its own heat and light by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core, which is what defines a star. It is about 150 million km from Earth; light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cover this, so it is about 8 light minutes away. It is a middle-sized yellow dwarf, about 1.4 million km across (about 109 Earth diameters), with a surface temperature of about 5 500 °C; some stars are far larger and brighter, but most (red dwarfs) are smaller, cooler and dimmer.

questions.question: Describe the Alpha Centauri system: name its members, state their distances and identify the nearest star to the Sun. Explain how to find Alpha Centauri in the South African sky.
questions.expected_answer: Alpha Centauri is a system of three stars. Alpha Centauri A (a yellow star slightly larger and brighter than the Sun) and Alpha Centauri B (slightly smaller and orange) orbit each other about every 80 years, about 4.37 light years away. Proxima Centauri, a small dim red dwarf with about an eighth of the Sun's mass, is about 4.24 light years away and is the nearest star to the Sun; it was discovered in 1915 by Robert Innes at the Union Observatory in Johannesburg. To the naked eye A and B appear as one bright golden star, the brighter of the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross, in Centaurus.

questions.question: Use a scale model or travel time to describe how far away the nearest stars are. Explain why looking at the stars is looking into the past, and state two factors that determine how bright a star appears.
questions.expected_answer: Proxima Centauri is about 40 trillion km away. If the Sun were a 22 cm soccer ball in Johannesburg, the Earth would be a 2 mm grain about 24 m away and the nearest star about 6 500 km away (about as far as Cairo), with almost nothing in between. Voyager 1 at about 17 km/s would take about 75 000 years to travel that far, while light (300 000 km/s) takes about 4.24 years. Because light takes time to travel, we see a star as it was when its light left it, for example Alpha Centauri as it was over four years ago. Apparent brightness depends on how much light the star gives off and on its distance (e.g. Beta Centauri looks about as bright as Alpha Centauri though about 90 times further away, because it gives off thousands of times more light than the Sun).
